power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: However, there is often a perceived gap between what has been acknowledged at a theoretical level and how it has been implemented and practised in reality (Mukherjee & Ghosh, 2022; Macfarlane & Ottewill, 2004).

text.text: One such discrepancy can be inferred from research into business students, who have frequently been compared with students from other schools or majors, not least in terms of their moral competence (Ghoshal, 2005; Mitroff, 2004).

text.text: This research has elicited an ongoing debate about the relative moral standing of business students versus non-business students.

On the one hand, some studies project an 'immoral' or 'unethical' image of business students: that they are more likely to practise deception for personal gain and apply egoism in ethical decision-making (Shank, 2018); they have a higher tendency for moral disengagement (Baker et al., 2006); they are more tolerant of unethical business practices compared with non-business students (Yu & Zhang, 2006); and they often engage in cheating behaviours (Parks-Leduc et al., 2022).
text.formatted: On the one hand, some studies project an 'immoral' or 'unethical' image of business students: that they are more likely to practise deception for personal gain and apply egoism in ethical decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Shank, 2018)</ref>; they have a higher tendency for moral disengagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2006)</ref>; they are more tolerant of unethical business practices compared with non-business students <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Yu & Zhang, 2006)</ref>; and they often engage in cheating behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Parks-Leduc et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our view, it is still open to debate whether those students are, indeed, somehow ethically compromised.

When previous studies are examined closely, it appears that most focus on a single character trait (e.g., a specific virtue/vice) or one aspect of moral development (e.g., Parks-Leduc et al., 2022; Shank, 2018; Wang et al., 2011).

text.text: The problem with focusing on a single trait or multiple specific traits is that it reduces students' perceived moral competence to a discrete box or boxes, while neglecting the fact that they are developing as holistic human persons.
As significant as individual character traits and virtues are, only a small subset of those cannot reflect the overall moral status of students.
Thus, there has been insufficient holistic exploration of students' moral excellence at a meta-virtue level, even within studies motivated by Aristotelian virtue ethics.

Such virtue ethics is gradually becoming the theory of choice within large segments of business ethics (Alzola et al., 2020; Sison & Redin, 2023), and we draw upon it as our theoretical foundation in this paper.

text.text: Because Aristotelian virtue ethics does not posit any single moral virtue as a prioritising master virtue (such as justice in Plato or ren in Confucianism), but contextualises all moral decision-making as being integrated through the intellectual meta-virtue of phronesis, any Aristotelian measure of moral competence will need to focus on the metacognitive, decision-making capacities of phronesis.

Yet despite the presumed significance within Aristotelian virtue ethics of phronesis (practical wisdom) in predicting ethical motivation and behaviour (Darnell et al., 2019; 2022; McLoughlin et al., 2025), few studies have examined this issue in the context of business education.

text.text: Although business students may appear to be demonstrating certain questionable characteristics, such as being excessively money-driven or greedy, this does not necessarily mean that they possess less well-cultivated phronesis compared with other groups of students.
Perhaps they may be greedier when facing temptations of a certain commercial kind, while remaining comparable to non-business students in overall moral functioning, for instance.

The present study aims to advance the ongoing debate about business students' degree of moral development by utilising a newly validated measure for multifaceted phronesis, the Short Phronesis Measure (SPM: McLoughlin et al., 2025).

text.text: Our study aims to respond to the ongoing debate on whether business students are morally less developed (or not) than their counterparts.

Our study also responds indirectly to the important question of whether business education is corrupting by nature, dragging down the moral level of those students who are studying at a business school.
We employ the SPM in order to treat moral functioning in an integrative manner, instead of other measures focusing on a single character or virtue or one aspect of morality.

Therefore, our work contributes to business ethics education research via the application of a more integrated moral-functioning lens, in a field so far largely dominated by a trait-by-trait measurement lens.

We deem the choice of a measure to be crucial here because our aim is to ameliorate gaps in the current literature on the relative moral competence of business versus nonbusiness students: literature that has so far been too selective and trait-specific.

Obviously, there are other measures of overall moral competence available, and our preference for the SPM is not only motivated by its rootedness in Aristotelian theorising, but also by the fact that business ethics is becoming increasingly driven by virtue ethics.

More specifically, we consider the SPM is the most suitable one for at least five reasons: 1) It is the only available short measure of phronesis; 2) standard Kohlbergian and neo-Kohlbergian measures focus exclusively on the rational element in decision-making and motivation, rather than the overall metacognitive aspects of moral functioning; 3) the widely used Values-in-Action (VIA) measure from positive psychology lacks an integrative higher-order virtue (e.g., practical wisdom), which is critically important for the integration of virtue, especially in cases of virtue conflicts; 3) the SPM is preferable to the currently fashionable Moral Foundations Theory measure because the SPM has been found to predict (inversely) the traits of the Dark Tetrad with more precision than Moral Foundation Theory; 5) the SPM predicts components of overall human flourishing; 6) business students' ethics is arguably even more important in the age of AI, and phronesis predicts positive usage of AI.
An elaboration of those six reasons can be found in McLoughlin et al. (2025 McLoughlin et al. ( , 2026)).

text.text: This is odd, given various recent efforts to enhance business ethics education, either through discrete taught curricula or embedded or 'caught' interventions.

It still remains something of a 'black box' whether business students have made any progress in terms of moral and ethical development of late, when compared with non-business students, especially given the fact that business ethics education seems to have acquired a higher profile in recent years, in the time of AI, than various other sub-disciplines of professional ethics.
To sum up, some previous research suggests an 'unhappy reading' when examining business students' moral development, especially when viewed through a virtue ethics, characterological lens.
Character-oriented studies tend to focus on one or a few select character traits in business students and then compare them with non-business students.
The limitations of this existing research were mentioned in the Introduction.
Other studies, employing non-virtue-ethical moral frameworks, have concentrated upon espoused moral attitudes or observable behaviour outcomes.

However, a lacuna in all those research traditions, within and outside of virtue ethics, is the failure to look more holistically at students' moral metacognitions or ability to balance competing moral demands.

This is even more remarkable given how many of the recent studies are motivated by Aristotelian virtue ethics; for according to such virtue ethics, the ultimate criterion of moral functioning in adults lies in the intellectual meta-virtue of phronesis (as already indicated).
This lacuna has inspired our phronesis-based research lens, as explained in the following sub-sections.
Virtue ethics is gradually superseding, or at least complementing, deontology and utilitarianism as the theory of choice within professional fields, not least business ethics.
Modern virtue ethics typically takes its inspiration from Aristotelian notions of character and virtue, although in the East, Confucian virtue ethics is also making a comeback (Alzola et al., 2020).

text.text: Several concepts central to the way Aristotle understood ethics are important components of modern virtue ethics theory.
These concepts are outlined by Aristotle in his Nicomachean Ethics (1985) and include eudaimonia (flourishing), arete (excellence or virtue), and phronesis (practical wisdom).
text.formatted: These concepts are outlined by <ref type="bibr">Aristotle in his Nicomachean Ethics (1985)</ref> and include eudaimonia (flourishing), arete (excellence or virtue), and phronesis (practical wisdom).

text.text: According to virtue ethics, an action is right if it exemplifies virtue, with such exemplification being conducive to or constitutive of human flourishing.

Thus, an action is right not because it is required as one's duty in accordance with a formalistic principle (as in deontology) or because it has desirable overall consequences (as in utilitarianism) but because it exhibits good character, which, in turn, promotes human flourishing.

In contrast to other moral theories, the concept of flourishing (and good character insofar as it promotes flourishing) is thus what is foundational in virtue ethics, rather than the concepts of duties or consequences; and what defines acting well is derivative or a matter of what is consistent with good character.

Within business ethics, in particular, what attracts theorists is virtue ethics' focus on how exhibiting the virtues is both conducive to and constitutive of good business practices and, more generally, promotes the ideal of virtuous professionalism in business.
When making this connection, many neo-Aristotelian business ethicists read Aristotle through a MacIntyrean lens (e.g., Sison & Redín, 2023).

text.text: Neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics is unique in positing that the most problematic choices facing ordinary people, most notably adolescents, young adults, and professionals, are not choices between vice and virtue but between different virtues when those seem to clash in the same situation (e.g., loyalty to colleagues versus honesty to your boss in potential whistleblowing scenarios).

Therefore, one of the intellectual virtues, namely phronesis or practical wisdom, acquires a unique meta-role (as it did in Aristotle's original virtue theory) as a coordinator and arbitrator: the conductor of the whole virtue orchestra, as it is sometimes put.
Phronesis is meant to oversee the moral values and virtues and provide them with the necessary checks and balances to secure overall ethically wise decisions.
This proposed meta-virtue can thus be defined as excellence in ethical decision-making.

It is concerned both with finding the correct 'golden mean' (i.e., the medial state between deficiency and excess) of a single virtue, when applied in complex contexts, and the proper interactivity, or balancing, of different virtues where those seem to call for different responses in the same situation.

For instance, is it possible to reconcile the commonly clashing demands of honesty and kindness by being kindly honest or honestly kind, or in a particular situation, may it call for the abandonment of one of the two virtues?
Whatever the eventual decision will be, it is the faculty of phronesis that is meant to do the adjudicative heavy lifting.

At the same time, it turns simple dispositions to be good along various independent paths into a coherent way of life, a comprehensive moral journey, guided by right reason, albeit a journey that is heavily contextualised and individualised (Kristjánsson & Fowers, 2024).

text.text: Phronesis has been undergoing a significant academic revival of late.

What we could call the new 'phronesis bandwagon' was originally driven by philosophers (e.g., Annas, 2011; Curzer, 2012; Russell, 2009), but this interest has also percolated to psychologists (Schwartz & Sharpe, 2011; Wright et al., 2020; Fowers et al., 2024) and theorists working within various branches of professional ethics, such as business (Alzola et al., 2020), medicine (Kaldjian, 2014) and nursing (Armstrong, 2007).

text.text: Their study was notable for employing confirmatory factor analysis within a structural equation modelling framework, using existing psychological instruments that were theoretically aligned with the APM's four domains.

While this approach lent initial empirical credibility to the model, it bypassed the exploratory phase typically used to assess how the structure might emerge from data organically, instead relying deferentially on Aristotelian theory.

Moreover, because the measures were adapted from unrelated domains and the item pool was neither designed specifically for phronesis nor made publicly available with scoring instructions, the study raised important concerns regarding how others might replicate the confirmatory model or use the measure in practice.
The lengthy nature of the instrument (45 minutes approx.) also constrained its utility for applied or large-scale research.
In response to these limitations, the Short Phronesis Measure (SPM) was invented by McLoughlin et al. (2025), based on the APM.

text.text: Upon its development, the measure was validated with a large-scale representative (census-matching) dataset collected from adult participants recruited in the USA and UK.
The SPM enables researchers to examine the multifaceted nature of phronesis in a feasible way due to its brevity.

It has also been found to predict various outcomes of interest (directly or inversely), including dark personality traits, moral disengagement, flourishing, and critical and ethical stances on the use of AI and emerging technologies (see McLoughlin et al., 2026).

text.text: However, from an Aristotelian perspective, such measures are doubly deficient, at least when the participants are of adolescent age or older.

First, while children can be considered adequately virtuous if they exhibit individual moral virtues such as honesty and compassion, adolescents and adults can only be considered to possess moral excellence if they are adept at resolving moral quandaries: i.e., dealing with situations that involve the apparent conflict of virtues.
Notably, the widely used VIA measure does not contain any discrete meta-virtue like phronesis.
Second, as we are not transparent to ourselves, measures of moral excellence should ideally not rely solely on self-reports.

This is why neo-Kohlbergians (see, e.g., Rest et al., 2000) suggested providing participants with moral dilemma scenarios for evaluation, for which answers could be deemed appropriate or not by comparing them with the verdict of an expert panel.

text.text: The most genuinely Aristotelian approach to measuring moral excellence in adults (including aspiring and practising professionals) is by homing in on their phronesis levels.

In the Aristotelian model, it is impossible to be practically wise without moral excellence (although it is possible to be amorally competent in calculating outcomes: what Aristotle referred to as the sub-virtue of deinotes or instrumental cleverness).
This is because the moral virtues provide phronesis with both substantive content and psychological motivation.

Conversely, it is impossible for adults to excel morally without phronesis, as in default of this vital intellectual virtue, they will flounder when confronted with the complex and often ambivalent rough and tumble of adult personal and professional life.
This explains further why we consider the recent Short Phronesis Measure, described above, the most suitable instrument to measure the moral excellence under scrutiny in this paper.

In this study, instead of comparing single or multiple character traits or certain dimensions of moral excellence (e.g., ethical attitudes), we compare the overall moral excellence of business and non-business students by using the recently validated SPM instrument, which synergises insights from both virtue ethics and moral psychology.

Numerous previous studies have attempted to uncover the 'myths' about business students versus non-business students from different angles or perspectives, yet none of them has employed a comprehensive approach with a meta-intellectual virtue lens to understand moral excellence and character functioning between those students.

For example, as already noted, most previous studies have either focused on one aspect of moral functioning, e.g., moral judgement and reasoning, or specific character traits, while failing to capture a holistic or orchestra-like view of moral excellence.
Hence, the implications of their findings might be limited or partial.

From a business ethics education perspective, over the past two decades, the importance of integrating ethical values into curricula has become a critical component in business school education (Issa & Pick, 2018), driven by the need to equip future entrepreneurs and managers with ethical excellence and a sustainable developmental mindset.

text.text: What was once a matter of individual school choice is now embedded in the expectations of major accreditation bodies such as AACSB, EQUIS, and AMBA.
This shift positions universities' efforts within a broader global movement in business education rather than as an isolated institutional practice.
However, the efforts and effectiveness of this integration may vary across institutions.

For example, some institutions engage with ethics, sustainability, and responsible management education genuinely; whereas in some cases, these elements may be introduced mainly to satisfy external expectations or accreditation requirements, without deeper reflection on how such values are actually developed, transferred, and assessed through the student learning experience.

The university under investigation in the present study has made deliberate efforts to integrate ethical values into its ethos, practices, and teaching, going beyond mandatory and optional courses by embedding ethics, ESG, sustainability, and responsible management across its curricula, assessment methods, and continuous quality improvement mechanisms -rather than merely documenting them in the accreditation process.

However, this does not represent the general status of other business schools in China, as the university under investigation is distinct with its internal features, such as a high percentage of international staff and exclusively English-speaking courses.
Our study explores differences in moral excellence, as defined by the SPM, which embraces cognitive, affective, perceptual, and motivational aspects.

Because this is believed to be the first study to employ the theoretical model in question and the resulting measure in a business ethics context, and the existing previous studies in the field have reported contradicting results, we employ a data-driven approach based on a Bayesian perspective rather than hypothesis-driven testing based on a frequentist perspective (Han, 2024a).

text.text: We expect that this data-driven exploration will show researchers in the field a holistic picture of the integrative understanding of moral and character functioning among business students (in comparison with non-business students), for further hypothesis-driven examinations and educational practice in business schools.

The participants in the study were students from a joint-venture university between a Chinese University and a UK university (English is the official teaching and learning language), located in southern China, with a predominantly local student body, though a small but growing international student body.
This university is distinct and does not represent the general status of Chinese higher education.
The reason that we chose this study context is that English is the official language, and teaching and learning activities are also in English.
This made it possible to administer a survey in English.
The study was approved by the first author's university Ethics Committee in December 2023.
A survey platform called Wenjuanxing (问卷星) was adopted to collect data, and the survey was advertised via school emails, student groups, and module leaders.
The participant information sheet and consent form were attached to the advertisements.
It took about 20-25 minutes to complete the survey.
As compensation for students' time and effort to participate in the study, a small number of lucky-draw e-coupons (about 30RMB or $4USD per/student) were provided.
The duration of the data collection was from February to July 2024.
By default, Wenjuanxing blocks duplicate submissions from the same logged-in user upon questionnaire publication.
The sample frame consisted of 1056 responses.

Among these, 403 were identified as invalid and excluded from further analysis for the sake of data reliability, mainly due to duplicated answers from the same IP address but with different user names.

Consequently, the response rate was 62%, and the final valid sample size was 653 (male:164 = 11%; female:489 = 89%) from business students (n = 289) and students from other schools (n = 364), for example, schools of humanities and social science, mathematics, and education.

text.text: The present paper focuses on analysing and reporting students' phronesis, or practical wisdom levels only; hence, we will concentrate on the SPM measure and leave the MGM out.
The SPM (McLoughlin et al., 2025) was developed as a purpose-built instrument grounded directly in the theoretical components of the APM.
text.formatted: The SPM <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(McLoughlin et al., 2025)</ref> was developed as a purpose-built instrument grounded directly in the theoretical components of the APM.

text.text: Crucially, it approached the measurement of phronesis inductively in the first instance (drawing on 4,000 representative adult US and UK respondents), using exploratory factor analysis to allow the data to shape the structure rather than imposing a theorised structure a priori.
This led to the identification of ten interrelated factors, constituting a refined framework referred to as the neo-APM.
Three of these dimensions relate logically to the idea of Moral Perception:

Moral Relevance (accurately recognising when an action reflects on one's character), Situational Moral Irrelevance (identifying when it does not), and Virtue Identification (discernment of which virtues apply in a given context).

Moral Emotion fractionates into Emotional Regulation (managing feelings in morally charged moments), Positive Moral Emotion (feeling good when doing good), and Negative Moral Emotion (feeling bad when acting immorally).

Two components relate to Moral Identity: Moral Self-Relevance (seeing morality as personally, not just socially, important) and Aspired Moral Identity (having an ideal moral self and striving toward it).

Finally, Moral Adjudication fractionates empirically into two dimensions known as Moral Deliberation (actively seeking relevant information before making a moral choice) and Moral Integration (coherently weighing all other components in the decision process).

This tenfactor structure preserves the spirit of the APM while extending it empirically, offering a more fine-grained and applicable understanding of phronesis, suitable for both research and practice.
Confirmatory analyses revealed that this model was a good fit to the data in the large representative samples of both the USA and the UK.
It was also shown to have good test-retest reliability and excellent criterion validity for predicting a wide range of personality, flourishing, and moral outcome variables.

text.text: According to them, the effect size corresponding to Cohen's d = .10 "indicates an effect that is very small for the explanation of single events but potentially consequential in the not-very-long run" (p. 156).

If the calculated ratio of the HDI overlapping with the ROPE was non-zero, we concluded that the evidence would not decisively support that the effect size of interest would be practically equivalent to zero.

In the current study, we explored the differences in ten subcomponents of phronesis assessed by the SPM across business and non-business students.

Our Bayesian regression analyses, used to explore the differences in a data-driven manner, showed that the null model, suggesting the non-significance of the group (business vs non-business) as a categorical predictor, could not be rejected, for any subcomponent.
In general, these findings offer novel insights into the debates regarding whether moral development among business students is significantly different from that among non-business students.
Previous studies have reported contradictory results.

For example, to reiterate, in some previous studies, business students are perceived as having more lenient attitudes towards cheating than non-business students (Simha et al., 2012; Smyth & Davis, 2004; Klein et al., 2007); and multiple studies suggest that business students cheat more frequently than non-business students (Simha et al., 2012; Smyth & Davis, 2004; Parks-Leduc et al., 2022; McCabe et al., 2006).

text.text: The issue here may be that the conventional conceptual and methodological approaches employed in the previous studies reporting the contradicting outcomes did not consider the holistic and multifaceted nature of moral motivation and behaviour.
The majority of previous studies and debates pertaining to business students' moral qualities tended to concentrate upon several 'cliché' character traits, such as greed or dishonesty.
They did not treat and examine the students as moral agents with moral excellence in a holistic manner.

Hence, given the results from the current study, we may need to re-evaluate the validity of the stereotypes about business students as being morally inferior to their counterparts who are not studying business.

Subsequently, we need to carefully examine the philosophical foundations and educational approaches to promoting their ethical and positive development effectively for their successful career as well as for their flourishing as human beings .

The phronesis model and its new measure, the SPM, inherited from Aristotle's theorising, will help us better navigate what should be pursued in business ethics education by providing us with novel theoretical and methodological insights.

For instance, it will allow researchers and educators to examine and evaluate the effectiveness of business ethics education in a holistic manner by addressing multifaceted moral functioning, which embraces cognitive, affective, and motivational aspects of human morality.

The research outcomes obtained with the comprehensive measure, the SPM, provide us with better insight into understanding and promoting ethical behaviour within the context of ethics education, compared with conventional measures focusing on certain aspects of moral functioning, such as the Defining Issues Test focusing on moral reasoning only (Choi et al., 2020).

text.text: According to Aristotelian virtue ethics, those virtues should already be in place from the students' earlier habituation phase.
If students have not acquired a character trait of compassion by the age of 18, there is probably not much that can be done about that in university classes of professional ethics.
However, phronesis is developed through late adolescence and early adulthood, so the time is ripe to foreground such development at the university level.

text.text: These previous research findings may explain the positive association between age, moral deliberation, moral self-relevance, situational moral irrelevance, and emotional regulation that we found.
Finally, the positive associations between education level and all phronesis components are consistent with previous research on higher education and moral development.
It has been shown that experience in higher education is significantly associated with sophisticated moral reasoning and related moral cognitive skills (for review, see King & Mayhew, 2002).

text.text: Future studies may be necessary to examine further details on why the significant results were not reported across all subscales in analyses involving participants' gender and age.
To recap, business school students showed no significant difference from nonbusiness students across all SPM subscales.
We do not consider this finding to stand in need of a specific explanation; if not because of some contradictory findings in the past, this is probably what most people would have expected anyway.

As Miller (1999) argued, business students do not come into business schools with a tendency or intention to be unethical or greedy, but rather they may be influenced by the principle of rational selfinterest values absorbed from finance and economics courses. Colby et al. (2011) highlighted that main business courses (e.g., marketing, management, finance, and accounting) are dominated by market-based analytic frameworks, and this leads to business students' uncritical application of these frameworks.

text.text: As a result, business students are often associated with certain specific negative character traits.
However, those traits may not negatively impact moral functioning across the board, as we have demonstrated.
These findings point to an educational implication worth further consideration.

While the study does not test whether specific curricular or co-curricular interventions directly cause ethical outcomes or develop virtue literacy, the results suggest that deliberate institutional efforts -such as the integration of ethical values through mandatory and optional modules -may play a supportive role in enriching students' virtue literacy (Jubilee Centre, 2022), an important precursor to ethical action.

This raises the possibility that business school educators could benefit from incorporating ethical values genuinely into their teaching and learning activities, such as curricula, through multiple channels, including curricular, co-curricular, and extracurricular activities, and that universities might consider policies and resources to support such integration across business schools and beyond.

Rather than viewing business education solely in terms of profit-making, one might also consider an educational ethos that aligns profit with societal development, mutual flourishing, and the common good.

This could include attention to professional development, interactive pedagogies, an explicit focus on character and ethics, training in social-emotional competence, modelling of character, classroom and behavioural management strategies, as well as community service or service learning (Berkowitz & Bier, 2007).

text.text: These remain open questions for future research and curriculum design rather than being directly implied by conclusions already demonstrated by the present study.

The present study was administered in English at an English-taught university, as the students were all capable of using English as a learning and communication language and met the language standard (e.g.
IELTS, TOEFL).
However, for the majority of participants, English is not their first language; future studies may consider translating SPM into Chinese and other languages.

Going beyond the language level, since ethical excellence is often bound to context and culture, future studies should not only consider validating the SPM by simply translating the instrument but also giving attention to its cultural fit.

Furthermore, for better comparison in the domains of situational moral irrelevance and virtue identification, which demonstrated 2log(BF) = .33 and -.76, respectively, collecting more data would be beneficial.

In all other domains, the absolute values of the resultant 2log(BF) values were above 2.00, indicating the presence of evidence significantly supporting either the null or alternative hypothesis compared to its counterpart.
Another limitation regards the disciplinary focus of this paper; this is a paper using tools of moral psychology in a business educational context.
However, this is not an educational paper, and hence we elide questions about the effects that business ethics education classes might have had on the business students.

Mountains of research in professional ethics have shown that professional ethical competence is mostly caught from the university environment, and later work environment and organisational culture, through 'osmosis' (Kristjánsson, 2024).

text.text: Phronesis will not be caught from a learning environment that is inimical to virtue development in general.

As Russell notes (2021, p. 17), the difficulties in learning phronesis are not only caused by its 'high intrinsic load' (the need to synthesise cognitively different values and virtues) but also by a 'high extrinsic load' (environments often full of misleading feedback and bad practices).
Conversely, a virtueconducive environment can facilitate the development of phronesis.
We have not considered the possibility here that the kind of business ethics education that the students in our study have received has influenced their phronesis scores.
It could well be that they do better than their counterparts in many older studies because of the high quality of their business ethics education.
We finally wish to acknowledge a possible theoretical and contextual limitation.

Our approach and outcome might seem to be undermotivated with respect to Aristotelian virtue ethics, in the sense that they do not presuppose Aristotle's famous 'reciprocity thesis', according to which the moral virtues require phronesis and phronesis requires the moral virtues.
Rather, we assume that business students could score high on overall phronesis while lacking some discrete moral virtues.
It must be noticed here that the reciprocity thesis is about the phronimos (the ideal person with full phronesis).
We, on the other hand, treat phronesis as a scalar concept (Fowers et al., 2024) and attempt to measure where participants are on the scale with respect to the 10 identified sub-factors.
text.formatted: We, on the other hand, treat phronesis as a scalar concept <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fowers et al., 2024)</ref> and attempt to measure where participants are on the scale with respect to the 10 identified sub-factors.

text.text: A non-phronimos could presumably, in the Aristotelian picture, have a decent standing on the phronesis scale but still lack some specific moral virtues by being, for example, too greedy.

That said, we acknowledge that future studies should ideally study phronesis in conjunction with specific moral virtues to figure out which particular moral virtues predict or do not predict a higher phronesis score with respect to specific phronesis components.

This might also, helpfully, lead to the identification of different 'phronesis profiles' of individuals with different combinations of strengths or weaknesses, when their different phronesis components and mastery of different moral virtues are explored collectively.
One possible contextual limitation in the differences between business and nonbusiness students relates to the nature of major choice in Chinese higher education.

Unlike the assumption of autonomous self-selection in some Western studies, students' majors in China are often shaped by parental expectations, admission scores, perceived employability, institutional allocation, and family views of prestige; consequently, 'business student' may be a weaker proxy for a distinctive self-selected moral or value orientation than the literature sometimes suggests, which could add nuance to the debate over selection versus socialisation.

All in all, if we follow Aristotle in considering phronesis as a proxy for moral functioning, we conclude that business students seem to have the same potential to be morally virtuous as other students, based on our study findings, despite the literature being filled with labels or descriptions about their moral deficiencies.

For example, when facing a morally challenging situation involving a choice between competing moral alternatives, our findings indicate that they would be at least as adept as other students in choosing the best course of action.

Thus, the stereotypes and negative labels applied to business students should be abandoned, acknowledging that business students can be educated equally towards virtuous conduct and a flourishing life as any other students.

We firmly believe that business students' moral potential can be enhanced further through business ethics education that incorporates character education in general and phronesis cultivation in particular at the university and school level, not least within the discipline of business ethics.
American character educationist Marvin Berkowitz often remarks that all good education should be good character education.
We would like to rephrase it here as: all good business education should be good business ethics education.
The university and business school should intentionally create a culture and design programmes that promote ethical competence and good conduct, promoting individual and societal flourishing.
There is an old saying in Chinese that there are no students who cannot be taught, only unskilled teachers.

Returning to existing debates about whether business degree courses effectively shape students' values to be money-driven or whether business schools attract students with certain character traits (e.g., greed, dishonesty) (Kristjánsson et al., 2017), our study has not directly offered any conclusive evidence one way or another.

text.text: What it has shown, however, is that worries about business students' inability to exhibit apt moral functioning may be vastly exaggerated.

For business schools, however, a more substantive approach would require clearer curriculum mapping, greater coherence across modules and school ethos, and a more holistic view of how students progressively acquire these ethical and responsible management capabilities.

The compulsory or elective distinction is therefore perhaps better understood as a technical curriculum design choice, whereas the more fundamental question is whether the integration is compliance-driven or genuinely educational in purpose.

This will require business school leaders, faculty, and programme designers to deliberately develop a strategy to advance business ethics education and to incorporate it thoughtfully into the school-wide ecosystem, identifying new avenues to better support their students' moral development that advance individual and collective flourishing.
